newsitem.title: ITALY: EU Commissioner takes Italy to task over telecoms.
newsitem.headline: EU Commissioner takes Italy to task over telecoms.

text.p: EU Commissioner Karel Van Miert took Italy to task on Monday for dragging its feet in adopting legislation to open up its telecommunications market to competition.

Van Miert told a parliamentary commission that Italy still had time to put the necessary laws in place by a deadline of January 1998, when the European Union is due to throw open the telecommunications market to global competition.
"If Italy does not pay attention to this it risks becoming a straggler," he said, adding: "Even Spain has overtaken you, it was the slow coach and it has overhauled you."
Spain is one of five countries -- the others are Portugal, Greece, Ireland and Luxembourg -- which have asked for more time to prepare for full-blown competition.

Van Miert said that Italian state telecoms group Stet could find itself penalised in the future if it sought a partnership with an international company before Italy brought its legislation regulating the industry up to date.

"If tomorrow Stet wants to get married I could only give my blessing to such a marriage if the Italian (telecoms) market has been opened up," Van Miert told reporters as he left the hearing of the lower house of parliament's transport commission.
Van Miert was particularly critical of the so-called interconnection fees charged by Stet -- which until recently enjoyed a monopoly -- to rival operators in return for access to the Stet network.
"If the charges stay too high the Commission will not be a passive spectator. This is not a threat but a stimulus to proceed in the right direction," he added.
Van Miert said interconnection charges in Italy were currently more than twice the average in the European Union.
The Commission has set a deadline of July 1 this year for all EU telecoms operators to publish tariffs and conditions governing interconnection.
Van Miert said that a newly appointed top management team at Stet had assured him that the deadline would be met.
"I must tell you that until recently I was hardly optimistic as to the chances of Italy, which has not respected any of its deadlines, respecting this one," he said.
Italy was the only country of the 11 which had not sought a temporary waiver of EU regulations which had failed to liberalise alternative telecom infrastructures.
Another missed deadline fell due in January this year -- that of notifying the commission of legislative plans to open public voice telephony to competition by January 1 1998.
Van Miert also said that Italy appeared not to be in a position to guarantee that enough new telephone numbers would be available for new operators from the beginning of July this year.

"I am extremely worried by the fact that in Italy nothing seems able to be in place on the date of July 1 1997, while this is totally indispensable for new voice telephony operators to be able to compete from next January," Van Miert said.
Belgium and Austria were also struggling to get the needed legislation in preparation for full-blown competition by next year, Van Miert said.
"In the case of these three (countries) I nevertheless believe that if the necessary priority is given during the next six months we can be ready by January 1," he said.
